title: 72-Hour Kit
description: The EU recommends every household be prepared to be self-sufficient for at least 72 hours. This checklist covers the essentials.
items: 3 litres of water per person per day (9 litres total per person)
3 days of non-perishable food per person
Manual can opener
First aid kit
Torch and spare batteries
Battery or hand-crank radio
Copies of important documents (ID, insurance, medical)
Cash in small denominations
Warm clothing and sturdy footwear
Emergency blanket
Basic medications and prescription drugs (3 day supply)
Mobile phone and portable charger
Whistle to signal for help
Dust masks or N95 respirators
Local map (paper)
Multi-tool or Swiss army knife
Lighter and waterproof matches
Basic hygiene supplies (toothbrush, soap, toilet paper)
Baby supplies if applicable (nappies, formula, food)
Pet food and supplies if applicable

title: 2-Week Home Stockpile
description: A 2-week supply gives you resilience against supply chain disruptions, power outages, illness, or local emergencies.
items: 14 litres of water per person minimum — note this does not account for cooking; rice and pasta absorb significant water so store more than you think you need
Water purification tablets or filter
Rice (at least 2kg per person)
Pasta (at least 2kg per person)
Tinned meat (chicken, tuna, sardines)
Tinned beans and lentils
Tinned vegetables
Tinned fruit
Cooking oil (1 litre minimum)
Salt, sugar, and basic spices
Oats or porridge
Dried milk powder
Honey or jam
Crackers or hardtack
Coffee, tea, and comfort foods
14 day supply of prescription medications
Vitamins and supplements
Spare fuel for cooking (gas canisters)
Camp stove or alternative cooking method
Solar panel or hand-crank generator for charging devices
Candles and lighters
Torches and spare batteries
Power bank (fully charged)
Basic first aid supplies
Personal wet wipes — conserves water for personal hygiene when water is scarce
Disposable plates, bowls, and plastic cutlery — eliminates washing up water
Hygiene supplies for 2 weeks
Bin bags and sanitation supplies
Pet food for 2 weeks if applicable

title: Vehicle Emergency Kit
description: Keep this in your vehicle at all times. Breakdowns and accidents happen without warning.
items: Reflective warning triangles (legally required in many European countries)
High-visibility vest (legally required in many European countries)
Jump leads or portable jump starter
Tyre repair kit or spare tyre
Tyre pressure gauge
Torch and spare batteries
First aid kit (legally required in some countries)
Fire extinguisher
Blanket or emergency sleeping bag
Bottled water (2 litres minimum)
Energy bars or snacks
Spare phone charger / car charger
Paper map of your region
Basic tool kit (screwdrivers, pliers, tape)
Window breaker / glass hammer — essential if power fails and doors or windows lock (especially critical in EVs which can lock all doors and windows automatically in a crash)
Tow rope
Ice scraper and de-icer (winter)
Shovel (winter / rural driving)
Handheld PMR446 radio — if mobile networks go down you need another way to communicate
Waterproof jacket
Spare cash
Copy of vehicle documents and insurance

title: Everyday Carry Bag (EDC)
description: Items you carry on your person every day. If something happens away from home you rely on what you have with you.
items: Mobile phone (fully charged)
Portable phone charger (power bank)
Cash in small denominations — in a power outage card machines don't work and many shops can't process payments at all
ID and essential cards
Swiss Army knife or legal multi-tool — check your local knife laws before carrying a folding blade
Small torch or torch on keyring
PMR446 handheld radio or small battery FM radio
Paracord bracelet or length of cordage
Small first aid kit (plasters, pain relief)
Any essential medication
Water bottle
Lighter or matches
Pen and small notepad
Local emergency numbers written down (not just in phone)

title: Bug Out Bag
description: A bag packed and ready to grab if you need to leave home quickly. Aim for 72 hours of self-sufficiency.
items: Backpack (comfortable, waterproof or with rain cover)
Water (1.5 litres minimum) and water filter or purification tablets
3 days of food (high calorie, lightweight — energy bars, dried food)
First aid kit (comprehensive)
Shelter (bivvy bag, tarp, or lightweight tent)
Sleeping bag or emergency blanket
Fire starting kit (lighter, matches, firesteel)
Torch and spare batteries or head torch
Multi-tool or knife
Paracord (at least 10 metres)
Paper maps of your local area and region
Compass
Copies of important documents in waterproof bag
Spare cash
Mobile phone and charger
Battery radio
Warm layers and waterproof jacket
Spare socks and underwear
Sturdy boots (wear them, don't pack them)
Hygiene kit (toothbrush, soap, toilet paper)
Prescription medications (minimum 7 days)
Whistle
Work gloves
Dust mask or N95
Duct tape
Note with emergency contacts, meeting points, and rally plan

title: Evacuation Plan
description: Having a plan before you need it means faster, calmer decisions under pressure.
items: Identify two exit routes from your home
Identify two exit routes from your neighbourhood
Agree on a primary meeting point close to home
Agree on a secondary meeting point further away
Identify an out-of-area contact everyone can call
Know the location of your nearest emergency shelter
Plan for family members who may be at work or school
Plan for elderly or mobility-impaired family members
Know how to turn off gas, water, and electricity at the mains
Keep vehicle fuel above half tank at all times
Know at least two routes out of your city or region
Have paper maps — do not rely only on GPS
Keep bug out bags ready and accessible
Practice the plan with all household members
Review and update the plan every 6 months

title: Family Reunification Plan
description: What happens if an emergency occurs when your family is separated — at work, school, or elsewhere?
items: Every family member knows the home address from memory
Every family member knows at least two emergency contact numbers from memory
Agree on a local meeting point near home (e.g. specific street corner)
Agree on a secondary meeting point further away
Know your children's school emergency and lockdown procedures
Know your workplace emergency procedures
Establish an out-of-area contact as a communication hub
Every family member knows who picks up the children if parents cannot
Children know not to go with strangers even if they claim to be sent by parents
Establish a safe word for emergencies
Write the plan down and give a copy to each family member
Practice the plan with children so it is familiar not frightening
Update the plan when circumstances change (new school, new job, new home)

title: Power Outage Preparation
description: Power outages can last hours or days. Preparation makes them manageable rather than dangerous.
items: Torches in every room with spare batteries
Candles and lighters (use carefully — fire risk)
Battery or hand-crank radio for emergency broadcasts
Power banks for mobile phones (keep them charged)
Solar charger for extended outages
Know how to manually open your garage door
Keep cash available (card machines will not work)
Know where your fuse box and mains switches are
Backup heating plan (wood burner, gas heater — ensure ventilation)
Blankets and warm clothing accessible
Water stored — pumping stations may lose power
Food that requires no cooking or minimal cooking
Camp stove and gas canisters for cooking
Cooler bags to keep refrigerated food cold longer
Know the number for your electricity network operator

When power goes out — unplug all major appliances and electronics. When the grid restores, green energy sources (solar, wind) cannot handle a sudden heavy load the way traditional power stations can. Switching everything back on at once can prevent or delay restoration.
Switch appliances back on gradually once power is confirmed stable
Sewer pumps may lose power during an outage — avoid flushing ground floor toilets if possible. A toilet blocker can prevent sewage backing up.
Be discreet about cooking — food smells carry and can attract unwanted attention from unprepared neighbours
If you have battery backup or a generator, be cautious about how visible this is to others
Check on elderly or vulnerable neighbours

title: Shelter in Place
description: Sometimes leaving is not the right option. Civil unrest, chemical incidents, or extreme weather may mean staying put is safer.
items: Sufficient water for the household for at least 2 weeks
Sufficient food for at least 2 weeks
Means to cook without gas or electricity
First aid kit and medical supplies
Prescription medications for at least 2 weeks
Battery radio for official emergency broadcasts
Means to seal windows and doors if required (tape, plastic sheeting)
Torches and candles
Backup heating or cooling if applicable
Entertainment and activities (books, cards, games) for morale
Maintain communications with trusted contacts
Know when official advice changes — have a way to receive updates
Secure your home — lock doors and windows
Be discreet about cooking — food smells signal that you have supplies. Cook at low heat, keep windows closed where possible.
Avoid showing visible signs of power or resources (lights, generator noise) — this can attract people who are desperate
Keep vehicles fuelled in case situation changes
Have a plan for when and how to leave if situation deteriorates

title: Heating Failure
description: Heating failure in winter is a serious risk, particularly for elderly people. Relevant across most of Europe.
items: Thermal underwear and base layers for every household member
Sleeping bags rated for cold temperatures
Extra blankets
Hot water bottles
Hand and body warmers (chemical)
Identify the warmest room in the house to consolidate into
Draft excluders for doors and windows
Portable gas heater (ensure adequate ventilation — CO risk)
Carbon monoxide detector
Wood burner or fireplace (if available) with dry firewood stored
Know the signs of hypothermia
Know how to safely use alternative heating
Check on elderly or vulnerable neighbours
Know the number for your heating engineer
Know where the stopcock is in case pipes freeze and burst

title: Home First Aid Kit
description: A well-stocked home first aid kit covers the majority of minor injuries and buys time in serious situations.
items: Assorted plasters / adhesive bandages
Sterile gauze pads (various sizes)
Rolled bandages (crepe and conforming)
Triangular bandage and safety pins
Medical tape (zinc oxide and micropore)
Scissors and tweezers
Disposable gloves (nitrile, multiple pairs)
Antiseptic wipes and solution
Wound closure strips / steri-strips
Eye wash and eye pads
Thermometer
Paracetamol and ibuprofen
Antihistamine tablets and cream
Rehydration sachets
Burn gel and non-stick dressings for burns
Cold pack (instant)
CPR face shield
First aid manual
Emergency contact numbers inside the kit lid

title: Trauma / IFAK Kit
description: An Individual First Aid Kit (IFAK) focused on life-threatening bleeding and trauma. Get trained before you need it.
items: Tourniquet (CAT or SOFTT-W) — know how to apply it
Chest seals (vented, x2) — know when to use them
Haemostatic gauze (e.g. QuikClot or Celox)
Pressure bandage (Israeli bandage or similar)
Nitrile gloves (multiple pairs)
Trauma shears
Nasopharyngeal airway (NPA) with lubricant — training required
Permanent marker (for writing tourniquet time on skin)
Foil emergency blanket
Completed a Trauma / TCCC / HABC first aid course
Kit stored in accessible location known to all household members
Kit inspected and restocked every 6 months
Expiry dates on all consumables checked

title: Medications and Prescriptions
description: Managing medications during an emergency is often overlooked. Plan ahead.
items: List of all household medications (name, dose, frequency, prescriber)
Minimum 2-week supply of all prescription medications
Store medications correctly (temperature, light — check labels)
Know expiry dates and rotate stock
Over-the-counter essentials: paracetamol, ibuprofen, antihistamine, antidiarrheal
Rehydration sachets
Any allergy medications (EpiPen if prescribed — check expiry)
Spare glasses or contact lens supplies if applicable
Medical alert information accessible (blood type, allergies, conditions)
Print a medication list from NHS app or ask pharmacy for a dispensing receipt — prescriptions are electronic, keep a physical copy with your documents
Spare batteries for medical devices (thermometer, blood glucose meter, hearing aids)
Consider non-battery alternatives for critical devices (e.g. mercury or infrared thermometer)
Know your nearest pharmacy opening hours — 24-hour pharmacies are rare outside cities, plan accordingly

title: Communications Plan
description: If phones and internet go down, do you have a plan? Agree on it before you need it.
items: Every household member knows the family meeting points
Every household member knows at least 2 contact numbers from memory
Agree on an out-of-area contact as a central communication hub
Agree on check-in times if separated (e.g. every 6 hours)
Battery or hand-crank radio to receive emergency broadcasts
Know your local emergency broadcast frequencies
PMR446 radios for local family / neighbourhood comms (no licence required)
Agree on a PMR446 channel for your group
Know where to find official emergency information in your country
Practice the plan so everyone knows it
Write it down — do not rely only on memory

title: Radio Setup Checklist
description: Getting your radio station ready for emergency communications.
items: Radio transceivers tested and working
Spare batteries or charging cables available
Antenna inspected and connections secure
Frequencies programmed and labelled
Local repeater details stored
PMR446 simplex channels agreed with your group
Know your local amateur radio emergency net frequency (if licensed)
Radio licence accessible if required
Log book available for recording contacts
Phonetic alphabet, Q-codes, and prowords reference available
Backup power for radio (battery bank, solar)
Radio manual stored with the equipment
Tested communications with at least one other person in your network

title: Neighbourhood / Community Network
description: A prepared community is stronger than a prepared individual. Know your neighbours.
items: Introduce yourself to your immediate neighbours
Know which neighbours have useful skills (medical, mechanical, radio)
Know which neighbours may need help (elderly, disabled, families with young children)
Share contact details with trusted neighbours
Agree on a neighbourhood check-in signal or plan
Identify a local meeting point for the neighbourhood
Share useful resources (tools, skills, space)
Agree on basic mutual aid principles with trusted neighbours
Consider a neighbourhood PMR446 or Meshtastic / MeshCore network
Know your local community emergency response resources
Join or establish a local preparedness group
Connected to RPN community for wider network support

title: Important Documents Checklist
description: In an emergency, having copies of your important documents can save enormous stress. Store originals safely and keep copies accessible.
items: Passport (all household members)
National ID card
Driving licence
Birth certificates
Marriage or civil partnership certificate
Insurance documents (home, contents, vehicle, life, health)
Vehicle registration documents
Property deeds or rental agreement
Bank account details and emergency contact numbers for banks
Utility account numbers and provider contact details
Medical records and repeat prescription details
Vaccination records
Pet microchip and vaccination records
Will and power of attorney (location known to trusted person)
Emergency contacts list (written, not just in phone)
Leave a copy of your emergency contacts and medical info on the fridge door — emergency services, social services, and paramedics routinely check the fridge when responding to an incident
Photos of all household members (useful if separated)
Photos of valuable possessions (insurance purposes)
All copies stored in waterproof bag or container
Digital backup stored securely offline (encrypted USB)
